## Two sentences worth keeping

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
Two sentences to take away. From the Multi100 paper: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. And notice what preregistration did and did not do for you today – it protected your choice from being opportunistic, but it gave your declared dot no special status inside the curve. You lived both halves: the declaration made your one path defensible, and the grid showed it was still just one path among 840. Declare your path, then show the space it sits in – the two moves go together. From Auspurg and Brüderl, the constructive recipe we followed: precise question, explicit assumptions, multiverse, sensitivity. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: same *conclusion* – seventy-four per cent in Multi100 – and same *number* – thirty-four. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
:::

::: notes
If the day had one sentence, it is this one. There is no privileged single analytical path – only justifiable ones, explored openly. And notice that you have already done the right thing once: you made one defensible choice, you wrote down your reason before running it, and you placed your answer inside the space of alternatives rather than pretending it was the only one. That is the transferable habit. Everything else today – the tooling, the estimand, the graph, the curve – was in its service.
:::

## What you take with you {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Yours now**: a preregistered, rendered report · an estimand and a causal graph you wrote yourself · two dots on the class curve, one explored and one declared
- **Read**: the three *Nature* 2026 papers [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial] · the glossary [@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms] · @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial · @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand · @LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne · @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic
- **Explore**: the ten companion modules (intro to R · Quarto documents · the statistics behind today · causal graphs · the multiverse debate · simulation · one claim at two levels · repositories & preregistration · git & GitHub) · the Multi100 data · `fixest` & `ggdag` docs
- **Keep going locally**: the research-software and open-research teams at your university · a ReproducibiliTea journal club near you
- Everything is on the course site, and everything is open – fork any of it

::: notes
Here is what goes home with you. A rendered report with a preregistration block in it, an estimand and a causal graph that you wrote for a real published claim, and a dot on the class curve. The website on screen holds everything else – the readings, the data, the companion modules, the specification-curve reading, and the full SCORE dossier on the paper if you want to dig further. Two pointers for keeping the habit alive wherever you work: most universities have a research-software engineering team and an open-research or library data service that run training exactly like today's, and ReproducibiliTea journal clubs meet in dozens of cities – if there is not one near you, they will help you start it.
:::
